item.text: {"verdicts":[{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0022-R02-E001","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"Mexico’s real GDP grew 3.2% in 2023; official multidimensional poverty fell from 43.2% in 2016 to 36.3% in 2022, lifting 5.4 million people out of poverty. Access to health and, to a lesser extent, the educational gap worsened. The World Bank identifies significant challenges involving productivity, crime and violence, informality, infrastructure, public services, finance, competition, and regulatory uncertainty.","notes":["The excerpt supports the figures, poverty reduction, worsened deprivations, and listed challenges.","“Persistent challenges” was narrowed to “significant challenges,” matching the excerpt."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0022-R02-E002","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"Mexico has a strong track record of macroeconomic stability supported by an independent central bank and sound financial sector. The World Bank identifies public-finance challenges involving higher state participation in growth, expanded social programs, efforts to improve public-service access and quality, infrastructure investment needs, and fiscal support to PEMEX; it says addressing these needs will require medium-term revenue-boosting reforms to preserve debt sustainability.","notes":["The excerpt supports the stability assessment, listed public-finance challenges, and need for revenue-boosting reforms.","“Public-finance pressures increased because of” was narrowed to “public-finance challenges involving,” because the excerpt lists challenges but does not establish that causal wording."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0022-R02-E003","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":["The 2023 table reports a fiscal balance of -4.3% of GDP, revenues of 22.2%, debt of 46.8%, primary balance of -1.0%, gross fixed capital investment growth of 18.0%, government consumption growth of 2.1%, and real GDP growth of 3.2%."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0022-R02-E004","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The World Bank notes that uncertainty around ongoing constitutional reforms may weigh on investment. It also states that rating agencies monitor fiscal pressures and political risk due to the judicial reform.","notes":["The excerpt supports an investment risk from constitutional-reform uncertainty and monitoring of fiscal pressures and judicial-reform-related political risk.","It does not state that judicial-reform uncertainty itself was a potential drag on investment, so that wording was narrowed."]}]}
